title: Integer
body:

---

`int`. Whole numbers, 4 bytes, roughly ±2 billion. An [[Atomic type]], and the default type
for anything you are counting.

The thing that makes `int` interesting in this course is that its arithmetic is **not** the
arithmetic you learned in school:

```c++
7 / 2      // 3, not 3.5. The fraction is discarded, not rounded.
7 % 2      // 1. The remainder.
-7 / 2     // -3, truncated toward zero
```

`/` truncating and `%` giving what is left over is the [[Division Algorithm]], and it is the
only tool the three exercises below need. `%` is how you test divisibility (`n % d == 0`),
extract digits (`n % 10`), wrap a value into a range (`i % size`), and check for even
(`n % 2 == 0`). Almost every first-year number puzzle is one of those four.

Variants exist (`short`, `long`, `unsigned`) and matter for range, not for behaviour.
Exceeding the range is **overflow**, and C++ does not warn you: the value silently wraps
around. What actually happens to the bits is two's complement, covered in
[[Integer Representation]] and [[Complements]] in [[COMPUTING MACHINERY]].

Mixing an `int` with a [[Double]] promotes the `int`, so `7 / 2.0` is `3.5` while `7 / 2` is
`3`. That one-character difference is a [[Logic Errors|logic error]] waiting to happen; see
[[Type casting]].

Where this goes next: [[Division Algorithm]] → [[GCD and LCM]] → [[Prime Number]], each built
out of the one before, and all three formalised in [[DISCRETE MATH]].
